Best Termite Control: Bait vs Liquid vs Heat Treatment

By Shaw's Pest Control  ·  Wichita, KS

What's the Best Termite Control Method for Subterranean Termites?

If you're comparing termite control options, you've probably seen conflicting claims. One company swears by bait stations. Another pushes liquid treatments. A third says only heat kills 100% of the colony. Here's the truth: the best termite control method depends on your home, the species you're dealing with, and whether you're treating an active infestation or preventing one. In Kansas—especially across Wichita and surrounding areas—we deal primarily with subterranean termites, which tunnel through soil to reach wood. Since 1987, Shaw's Pest Control has held three state certifications and Master Tech Certification, and we've seen what works long-term. This guide breaks down the three main treatment types, explains which scenarios call for each, and gives you the questions to ask before signing any contract.

Understanding the Three Main Termite Treatment Methods

The best termite control approach comes down to three proven methods: liquid soil treatments, bait monitoring systems, and heat or fumigation. Liquid termiticides create a treated zone in the soil around and beneath your foundation. When termites tunnel through treated soil, they're exposed to the active ingredient and carry it back to the colony. Modern non-repellent liquids like fipronil work especially well because termites can't detect the chemical—they pass through it, share it during grooming, and the entire colony is affected over weeks.

Bait systems use monitoring stations installed around your property's perimeter. These contain wood or cellulose that termites prefer. Once activity is detected, the bait matrix is replaced with a slow-acting toxicant. Worker termites consume it and share it with the colony, including the queen. This method takes longer—typically 3 to 6 months—but uses far less chemical overall.

Heat and fumigation are reserved for drywood termites (rare in Kansas) or severe, widespread infestations inside a structure. Whole-structure heat treatment raises interior temps to 120–140°F for several hours, killing termites in all life stages. Fumigation tents the home and uses gas penetration. Both are invasive and expensive, usually considered last-resort options for subterranean termite control.

Which Method Works Best for Kansas Subterranean Termites?

For subterranean termites—the species that account for nearly all termite damage in the Midwest—liquid soil treatments remain the gold standard. These termites must return to soil for moisture, which makes a continuous chemical barrier highly effective. A properly applied liquid treatment lasts 5 to 10 years depending on the product and soil conditions, and it provides immediate protection.

Bait systems are ideal for homeowners who want minimal chemical use or have wells, gardens, or environmental concerns near the foundation. They're also effective as a monitoring tool even after a liquid treatment. The tradeoff is time: baits don't provide instant protection, and they require regular inspections to confirm the colony is eliminated.

Heat treatments don't apply to most subterranean cases. Because these termites live in the soil—not just the wood—heating the interior won't reach the source. You might kill the workers currently feeding inside, but the colony will send replacements within days.

If you're comparing bids and a company only offers one method, that's a red flag. The best termite control starts with a thorough inspection. Shaw's Pest Control evaluates infestation severity, moisture sources, structural access, and your property's unique conditions before recommending a treatment plan. Sometimes a combination approach—liquid treatment with bait monitoring—provides the best long-term protection.

What to Ask Any Pest Company Before Signing a Contract

Before committing to any termite control service, ask these questions. First: What species of termite do I have, and how did you confirm it? Subterranean, drywood, and dampwood termites require different treatments. A company should identify the species during inspection—not guess.

Second: What product are you using, and how long does it last? For liquid treatments, ask whether it's repellent or non-repellent, and request documentation on the product's proven longevity. For baits, ask what active ingredient is used once activity is detected, and how often stations are monitored.

Third: Does your treatment come with a warranty or damage guarantee? Reputable companies back their work. Understand what's covered, for how long, and what annual inspections or retreatments are included.

Fourth: Are your technicians certified? In Kansas, applicators must hold state certification. Companies with Master Tech Certification and multiple state licenses demonstrate a higher standard of training and accountability.

Finally: What prep work is required, and will you repair damage? Liquid treatments may require drilling, trenching, or moving landscaping. Heat treatments need clearing furniture and removing heat-sensitive items. Clarify who's responsible for repairs and lawn restoration. If a company rushes the estimate or pressures you to sign same-day, walk away.

Termite Treatment Considerations for Wichita and the Surrounding Area

Wichita sits in a moderate-to-heavy termite pressure zone, which means subterranean termites are active year-round when soil temps stay above 50°F. Our clay-heavy soils retain moisture well, which termites need to survive—but that same soil can make liquid treatments tricky if not applied correctly. Soil type, drainage patterns, and foundation design all affect how termiticides spread and bond.

Homes in Derby, Andover, and Maize often have crawl spaces or slab foundations with minimal clearance, which complicates inspections and treatment access. Older homes in El Dorado and Augusta may have untreated wood in contact with soil—a common entry point. A local pest control company familiar with Kansas construction styles and soil conditions will spot vulnerabilities a national chain might miss. That's why Shaw's Pest Control has served this area since 1987—we know how termites behave in our climate and how local homes are built.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the most effective termite treatment?

Liquid soil treatments using non-repellent termiticides are the most effective method for subterranean termites. They create a continuous barrier that termites can't detect, allowing the chemical to spread through the colony. When applied correctly and combined with moisture control, liquid treatments can protect a home for 5 to 10 years and provide faster results than bait systems.

How long does termite bait take to work?

Termite bait systems typically take 3 to 6 months to eliminate a colony. The process requires termites to find the bait, consume it, and share it with nestmates through feeding and grooming. Bait works slower than liquid treatments but uses significantly less pesticide and can be highly effective for environmentally sensitive sites or ongoing monitoring.

Can termites come back after treatment?

Yes, termites can return after treatment if the chemical barrier degrades, new colonies form nearby, or conducive conditions like wood-to-soil contact and moisture problems aren't corrected. This is why warranties and annual inspections matter. The best termite control includes both treatment and prevention—fixing leaks, improving drainage, and removing wood debris from around the foundation.

Is heat treatment better than liquid for termites?

Heat treatment is not better for subterranean termites. While heat can kill termites inside the structure during treatment, it doesn't reach the underground colony, which will send new workers back within days. Heat is best suited for drywood termites that live entirely within the wood. For Kansas homes dealing with subterranean species, liquid or bait treatments target the source.

Do I need a termite bond or warranty?

A termite warranty (often called a bond) provides ongoing coverage if termites return after treatment. Most reputable companies offer annual renewal agreements that include inspections and retreatment if needed. It's especially valuable for real estate transactions and long-term protection. Make sure you understand what's covered—some warranties include repair costs for new damage, while others only cover retreatment.

How much does professional termite control cost?

Professional termite treatment costs typically range from $1,500 to $3,500 for an average-sized home, depending on treatment method, infestation severity, and home size. Liquid treatments are usually a one-time cost with optional annual renewals. Bait systems often require lower upfront costs but ongoing monitoring fees. Always get multiple quotes and compare warranties, not just prices.
